### Regarding our democratic experiment in self government
  
Running for my local water board[1] has been an exercise in practicing the responsibilities and opportunities that freedom affords. I'm grategul to live in a community that has a tradition of civic life and folks volunteering their time. There is a small d democratic culture here in my tiny foothill town in the Crescenta Valley above the foothills of Los Angeles, not least because there's a void as an unicorporated part of LA County (so there's no local city and a bunch of confusingly overlapping local governments).[2]

Yesterday I had five friends and family out with me canvassing door to door. There is something grounding about going through the exercise in ringing a strangers doorbell, attempting to strike up a conversation, and build a connection. So many of the issues have nothing to do with what The Discourse has to say about the issues. From that worms eye perspective the big things are politics intruding upon someones Saturday morning and whether they feel like getting up from watching a game or their morning to come say hi to a stranger at the door. Some folks are amenable to a conversation, some want nothing to do with nobody. 

I am very much grateful for those conversations. A legend in local governance on both the elected and staff side shared that they enjoyed knocking on doors. I can see why. There is something fun about meeting new people, rediscovering your community and engaging in dialogue. That's what I enjoy at least. If I didn't have two small kids at home and high priorities, I would probably too take the time to go out every weekend and knock on all the doors. 

I met a pair of neighbors. One volunteered they were a Republican. The other offered that they were Very Liberal. To some eyes in the discourse they would have looked very similar, and talking about water issues they had fairly similar questions about what I planned to do to keep water rates low. (I shared about the [CV stormwater project that saves lower cost water locally.)](https://www.change.org/p/tell-ladwp-to-stop-wasting-crescenta-valley-s-stormwater/dashboard?source_location=user_profile_started) The left leaning gentleman had more to say about his time in high school and also the WPA programs that built the flood control channel. The right leaning gentleman had more to say about UCLA and the game yesterday. 

Looking out at politics these days, so much feels scrambled. Folks get a lot of their news and discourse online, sometimes in very suboptimal places, like Cloud Emperor Zuckerberg's Facebook which is optimized for digital advertising and commerce. I have engaged a lot on the local FB group that has ~1700 folks participating and very light moderation. At one point I was called a bot. I am 99.9% sure some of the folks there are bot with their stock photos and bizarre non-sequitors. Or maybe I am just betraying my millenial techie biases as folks share in Boomer and older mannerisms.[3] 

Something does definitely very very awry. The old signposts of civic life continue on though there's a need to pass the torch. The implicit protocol for public meetings, like a recent fire safety council one, is a monthly or bimonthly in person get together plus lots of information shared on dead pieces of trees. Those tend to be well moderated and have a substrate of civility. Then there's what happens online where there can be name calling and all the stuff that you see in what passes for civic discourse at the national level these days. 

My optimism about civic life stems from the ability to make change in my own backyard.[4] I am grateful for the opportunity to focus on something I can control. So much of politics these days feels like an outlet for Other Stuff, a lot of angst and resentment and anger and other things that collide as the digital world blurs together public and private life, placing a photo from a reunion or another person's grandkids next to an emotively engaging exhortation about the end of the world through war or ai or a school shooting. 

We are living through the end of Truth, Justice and the American Way. Or the death of one and the possible rebirth of another. I met young folk who clearly were living at home post high school or college and judging by their pajamas on a 2 PM on a Saturday (a snap reaction I know), were perhaps a bit adrift. There is very much a lost generation element, both in terms of folks struggling to find their way as folks work dead end service sector jobs. Or meeting folks at my 20 year high school reunion who did all the right (tm) things we were told to do growing up like keep your nose clean, go to college, get a good job, get married but then having kids and providing a home to raise a family can feel like Mount Everest. 

Spending time with older generations, I am reminded of the adage that the past is a foreign country. I watched a movie about the Apollo program a few years back with my dad and was struck by how everyone had a certain phenotype. Also the dress, the lifeways, really everything was so different. People here in that Baby Boom or Silent Generation who came to the Crescenta Valley had a whole different set of struggles and challenges. Now to simplify and exaggerate, there are a lot of older folks aging in place with very large homes and very low property tax payments. 

I am grateful that I did not have to go through a draft like many in those generations. I am very much saddened to see folks in my generation go abroad into forever wars, including a guy from my high school football team who has a rememberance marker at a nearby pocket park, one of those who never made it home. So much has changed in the twenty years since I graduated high school and yet so little. There is a strong passionate desire to preserve our little town that I love so dearly. 

I am reminded though of something my college football coach would say. You're either getting better or you're getting worse. Staying the same is an illusion. That local legend I mentioned who knocked on a zillion doors was famous earlier in his career for taking a staid bureaucratic process, the California general plan, which many civil servants take as a box checking exercise every few years and using it as an opportunity for genuine civic engagement. That plan formed the foundation for the renewal of the Pasadena Old Town which is a regional and in many ways worldwide gem. 

I see opportunities for that in La Crescenta as the conversations about the future of our community, of which water is a part, focus reactively on a few hot button developments rather that proactively about what we want our community to be. Freedom comes with responsibility. I would much rather our community chart our own destiny rather than have one-size-fits-all-mandates dictate our future. 

That conversation though feels deeply broken though perhaps at the start of something constructive. My friends from high school, the Crescenta Valley diaspora, all to a T pretty much love the idea of more housing to address the cost pressure they personally feel. The older generation here is worried about disruption to their way of life. In many ways all the craziness at the national and increasingly bleeding into the state and local level seems downstream of how our POTUS proclaimed "the American dream is dead."[5]

I am reminded though of something that VGR said which is trite but true in the battle of the generations discourse. Millenials are largely born to Boomers. People want their kids to succeed. There is hope in those messy mixed up opportunities for indidual action and people finding ways to adapt. Our little family is very lucky in that we remodeled my wife's childhood home and built an ADU for my in laws in the backyard, saving a pretty penny. I'm glad to avoid paying monopoly money for a fixer upper starter home.

More than anything, I am glad for the opportunity to engage and focus on something that I can actually control and potentially get done. I think there is much more need for that type of small d-democratic action and activity. So much of what makes America awesome rests on implict protocols and norms that go beyond formal voting. The Constitution begins with the words "We the People" for a reason. 

More to come and thanks for reading. 

***

[1]Well actually one of the local water boards because they overlap and nothing is simple in California water. 

[2]Or maybe that's just my competative former football player side of me speaking up. 

[3] Before the campaign, a year or two back, I saw a digital mob form about a mythical homeless person in a canyon that goes between where my parents' place and my house. I'm 99.99999% sure that whole thing was sparked  by teenagers hanging out down there and leaving the remants of their fire as kindling for speculative idle imaginations.

[4] In true Panglossian fashion, I have been enjoying tending my literal garden :) 

[5] I wrote a book once upon a time called A New California Dream so am feeling prescient hehehe :P well in some ways. I definitely did not have the world figured out in my early twenties though do think I had my finger on trends like the scrambling of life scripts and state capacity shortcomings ahead of the curve.
